# Things you might have thought before…

![](images/26-Why%20linguistics_2.png)



* Linguists are people who speak lots of languages?
  * But now you know that we’re just people who study language systematically\, whether we speak certain ones or not
  * Linguistics = scientific study of language
* English has five vowels – a\, e\, i\, o\, and u \(and sometimes y\)?
  * But now you know English has a lot more than that\!
  * IPA = one\-to\-one correspondence\!

---


![](images/26-Why%20linguistics_3.jpg)



* Parrots talk\, just like humans?
  * But now you know that things like arbitrariness\, creativity\, permitting displacement\, etc\. are hallmarks of a language\, and most animal communication systems lack at least one of these elements\!
  * A mode ≠ a system
* Dialects are bad; everyone should speak the standard?
  * But now you know that all language varieties are systematic and serve the needs of their speakers
  * And you know that no one speaks the same way all the time
  * AND you know that if dialects didn’t accomplish  _something _ for speakers\, people would stop using them
  * AND you know that the standard is hard to define
  * Dialects are languages\!

# Your Linguistics Journey!



* Many will need to take another linguistics class to satisfy a requirement – cool\!
  * Many will take LIN 200 = UK Core Arts and Creativity
  * Others often take one of our 300\-level courses\, especially LIN 331 = UK Core US Citizenship
* Maybe you had your “finding linguistics” moment in this class – awesome\!
  * If you are thinking about adding the major/minor\, you’ll need to take LIN 221 \(the other intro class…\)
  * But LIN 211 still “counts” as other LIN courses
* Maybe you just took this class for fun – sweet\!
  * Even if you don’t intend to major/minor\, you can take more classes that interest you\!
  * And…many people who go on to pursue graduate degrees in linguistics do not have UG degrees in it
::: {.notes}

Part of what we’ve done is teach you to think about language like a linguist
This requires a level of analysis that differs (sometimes drastically) from how everyday people think about language
You can now look at language as more than a collection of sounds and words
You know that there are rules, and that we can predict the kinds of language we’ll hear because it’s not haphazard


:::
